chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated to us. He said: My father narrated to us from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn Umar al-Jurjani. He said: Al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad, peace be upon him, said:

The first congregational prayer came about when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, was praying with the Commander of the Faithful Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him. Abu Talib passed by him with Ja'far and said: 'O my son, join the wing of your cousin.' When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, sensed him, he stepped forward to lead them both. Abu Talib departed joyfully, and he was saying:

'Indeed Ali and Ja'far are my two trustees / When the hardships of time and calamity strike. / By Allah, I will not abandon the Prophet, / Nor will any son of mine of noble lineage abandon him. / Do not abandon him, and support your cousin — / He is my brother through my mother among them, and my father.'
He said: That was the first congregational prayer that gathered on that day.

key_terms.جَمَاعَة: Congregational prayer; communal worship led by an imam
key_terms.جَنَاح: Wing; metaphor for support, strength, or companionship
key_terms.مُلِمّ: Overwhelming calamity; a pressing affliction of the times

ai.seo_question: What is the origin of the first congregational prayer in Islam according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith recounts the origin of the first congregational (jama'a) prayer in Islam. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) narrates that the Prophet Muhammad (SAWW) was praying with Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS) when Abu Talib passed by with his son Ja'far. Abu Talib instructed Ja'far to join his cousin in prayer, using the metaphor 'join the wing of your cousin.' When the Prophet sensed Ja'far's presence, he stepped forward to lead them both, establishing the first congregational prayer. Abu Talib departed joyfully and recited poetry expressing his unwavering support for the Prophet and his trust in Ali and Ja'far. This account is significant in Shi'a tradition as it demonstrates Abu Talib's awareness of and support for the Prophet's mission from its earliest days.
